#6819. Before & After: Dark, Underutilized Storage Spaces Make Way for a Cozy Library, Breakfast Nook, and Family Room

An intentional gut renovation turned dead space into room for a growing family.

With certain homes, it can take time (and a designer’s eye) to realize the full potential. For some, that means living within a less-than-perfect layout for a while to really understand the pain points. When a couple with twin boys bought this Greek Revival farmhouse in Connecticut’s tony Fairfield County in 2022, they knew changes were in store down the line.

“It didn’t feel like them yet,” says the project’s interior designer, Vivian Shao Chen. “The house was in great condition, but the layout didn’t work for how they lived.” The 1940s home had a considerable amount of dead space, including entire rooms and shadowy corners that felt disconnected from the rest of the home.

On top of that, planning a rework around the two youngsters was an additional challenge. “The question was always how a space can grow with them: what deserves the investment and what should stay flexible,” Chen adds.

Once Chen began working on the project in 2024, she refocused the homeowners' attention away from the idea of a home addition and sparse, “Scandinavian beach house” aesthetic toward a warmer, more traditional sensibility in line with the house’s original period style.

“I always start with trying to understand existing site conditions as much as possible,” Chen says. “What is the architectural language of the house? Where is it inconsistent, what can we edit? Often, very small but thoughtful changes can make all the difference.”

Ultimately, a gut renovation was necessary to address the home’s layout limitations, and new millwork was added throughout to provide character and a strong visual throughline. Now, each space has its own unique identity and every corner is packed with purpose—with plenty of wiggle room to allow for the young family’s necessary changes over time.

“This house feels so warm, cozy, and grounding,” Chen says. “Our hope is that we've designed for their current season of life and set a good foundation for the future without overdesigning, leaving room for the house to change as life does.”

FAST FACTSDesigner: Vivian Shao ChenContractor: The O'Dell GroupStylist: Andrew Carter ThomasLocation: Weston, CTThe Space: A three-bedroom, four-and-a-half-bath home across 4,218 square feet

A formerly nondescript pass-through area, the home’s entry now gives visitors a proper greeting with its lush Sandberg wallpaper bridging indoors and out. “It speaks to the beautiful Connecticut setting we are in and also says, ‘Welcome, come in and relax, it’s not too formal here,’” notes Chen.

Additionally, choosing darker tones in a foyer or hallway is a great way to emphasize an airier mood elsewhere. “These transition spaces are meant to feel cozy, enveloping and a little moody, so when you step into the open expanse of the living room, with all its light and views, the house seems to exhale,” the designer adds.

One space that was spared a major redesign was the living room, as its existing architecture already suited the household’s needs. “The living room has always been a breath of fresh air in the house, being the first big expanse you walk into, with wonderful views out onto the property and beautiful daylight,” Chen attests.

A touch-up was still in order, though. Chen refreshed the wall color and chose updated furnishings upholstered in velvet and linen to complement the family’s antique Chinese chest, which became the natural focal point in the room. “The contrasting elements balance out the lightness of the room in a way that feels quiet and grounding,” she adds.

One of the biggest triumphs of a home renovation is when an awkward spare room becomes the new go-to gathering spot—and that’s exactly what happened with this former storage space-turned-library.

Chen removed an en suite powder room, which helped anchor the layout around a seating area instead of feeling transitory. She then wrapped the room in quarter-sawn white oak millwork, which layered in all the stately personality that the former space was missing.

The millwork, while providing shelving and storage opportunities, also included a media center, a built-in desk, and a daybed. “The daybed cushions are intentionally sized like twin mattresses, so with a fitted sheet they become an extra bed for guests or sleepovers,” Chen says.

The space is now appropriately flexible, able to be cordoned off from the main living room with pocket doors or inviting enough for games or movies, with classic library sconces that make it especially cozy at night.

“The kitchen was a gut renovation, but in reviewing the layout, I felt like the bones were mostly right,” Chen muses. “It just needed a lot of editing and new finishes.” Without altering the footprint, Chen maximized the flow of the space by removing the ceiling beams, relocating the refrigerator, scaling up the windows overlooking the yard, and adding interior windows to open up views to the adjacent mudroom and breakfast room.

Then there was the kitchen island: a solid white oak piece on custom turned legs, topped with a seamless Calacatta Monet slab that Chen calls “sublime.” Overhead, an artful single pendant by Roll & Hill adds a far more impactful ambiance than a trio ever could. “It’s about finding restraint and negative space where it can make an impact,” Chen notes.

One notable omission in the cook space is the presence of upper cabinets—Chen chose hutch cabinets instead that “hide a microwave, a pantry, and a coffee station.” Apart from the millwork, finishes, and fixtures, the kitchen also includes all-new appliances, aside from the statement-making blue La Cornue range that was already in the home.

Even if breakfasting outdoors is only realistic for a few months in the Northeast, this nook right off the kitchen now provides the illusion of alfresco enjoyment. Originally, the room felt too out of step with the rest of the home, and even its most desirable feature—the view out of the picture window—was hard to appreciate in such a segmented space.

Chen reimagined the room as an interior porch, replacing the entry wall with a muntin division to lure guests from the kitchen to this sunny spot. The nook’s newly added bay windows provide more light and dimension, and its nickel-gap paneling has a soft, rustic touch. Chen also tucked a built-in banquette into the bay for the most obvious purpose: “You're now sitting in the view, not just looking at it.”

Through the breakfast room (and another set of muntin dividers) is the cozy, cocooning dining room. Rather than flooding this windowless room with light, Chen employed a clever strategy to maximize the ambiance. “The custom plaster finish on the walls and ceiling has a subtle sheen that catches the light, so what was once the room's drawback is now its greatest charm,” she notes.

Basements without a proper design outlook are destined to become clutter overflow areas. That’s exactly what was happening on the home’s lower level, so a gut renovation was in order.

To make the space more livable, Chen added millwork to conceal laundry and utility access, plush furnishings, and a new door and windows that open up to a walk-out terrace. Though the low ceiling had to stay, new nickel-gap paneling makes the space feel cozy rather than cramped. “The room reads as a true family room,” she says.

The former mudroom was a rough-and-tumble catch-all passage, but considering that this area functions as the family’s main entrance, it deserved a gut renovation that they could take pride in—starting with the floor. Chen swapped out the no-nonsense tile for a striking limestone checkerboard. “The light squares are actually the same limestone as the kitchen floor, only done in a different pattern,” she says.

New lockers and coat cabinets along the perimeter conceal all the out-the-door essentials, while a floating console, clad in drab olive, has the look of an antique find but was custom-made for the space. It functions as the necessary landing zone that every bustling family home needs; Chen intentionally kept the bottom open for sliding packages and storage baskets (and perhaps the odd shoe) out of the way.

This office bathroom was previously awash in neutrals but still managed to look dark and drab, so Chen revitalized it with a much-needed dose of drama. Her go-to design reference? Old New York members’ clubs.

“Instead of wrapping the room in dark wood, we kept the stained wood to the custom vanity and let color and pattern do the rest,” she notes. Outfitted with the white penny-tile floor, striped zellige in the shower, and racing-green color drenching, the space now nods to tradition while keeping it playful.

“The primary bedroom already had so much going for it: beautiful windows, generous proportions, and absolutely peaceful,” Chen attests. “Our goal was to keep and elevate those qualities.”

Chen amplified the room’s natural daylight with a fresh coat of Farrow & Ball's Slipper Satin, then softened the space with more natural textures, including a slipcovered linen bed, woven linen for the drapery, and a textured wool rug. Even though the bedroom has one of the most restrained palettes in the whole home, it celebrates textural variation.

To maintain the same serene but texturally rich feel as the adjoining primary bedroom, the bathroom needed a layout and material rework. To make the most of a modest footprint, Chen opted for slim Shaker linen cabinets and a floating vanity. “Seeing the floor continue beneath it tricks the eye, making the room feel larger than its actual standing space,” she says.

The room’s warm marble floors and soft off-white color also provide an ideal backdrop for the room’s showstopper moment: a Calacatta Viola slab shower and backsplash, with deep, wine-toned veining.

For now, the twin boys share this bedroom, so the existing architecture was left alone. Instead, the focus was on enriching the palette with taupe, cream, blue, and copper tones and choosing furnishings that can flex over time. “The art is by the boys themselves, which was so special to incorporate into the room,” says Chen.

Vivian Shao Chen is an interior designer specializing in whole-home designs, including interior architecture. She has over 15 years of architectural training and professional experience, and focuses on residential interiors and lifestyle design, including home goods and clothing.

#6815. All Aboard Fashion’s Absurd Hat Train

Swim caps and train conductor hats: The runway’s most theatrical headwear is made for standing out.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Fashion can’t get enough of freaky hats lately. Following the main character hat trend from a few seasons past, this time headwear has gone totally theatrical and over-the-top. Between Chanel’s fin-embellished Nemo-esque swim caps and Junya Watanabe’s super camp, oversize ’70s baker-boy-style caps, headpieces are seemingly obsessed with transforming their wearers into outlandish personas. And at a time when clothing is centered on escapism and storytelling, an eccentric chapeau might just be the most perfect finishing touch.

Simone Rocha’s sequin-embellished bonnets with chin straps might turn you into a living doll. Celebs, too, have already gotten the memo: Elle Fanning recently wore a Stephen Jones-designed makeup compact headpiece to match her Givenchy dress inspired by an archival piece he created over three decades ago, while doing press for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping. Elsewhere, Cardi B showed up in a white embellished gown from Tamara Ralph’s spring 2026 couture collection, styled with a huge, showgirl-style feather hat. Ciara walked the Junya Watanabe spring/summer 2027 runway while wearing a bedazzled helmet dripping with chains.

At Vaquera’s spring/summer 2027 show titled “I’m a put-on-a-show kind of girl,” the neon high-octane gowns were counterbalanced with huge, satirical boater hats, followed by a weird and whimsical chef hat and maid headpiece paired with shrunken, mini bloomer uniform onesies. Adding more humor to the collection, the designers ended the show by performing a live karaoke version of Sonny & Cher’s “I Got You Babe.” The brand is the king of the theatrical character hat. For fall/winter 2026, it showcased pillbox-style hats that eclipsed the face with cutouts for the eyes, fencing-mask-inspired headwear, and an elongated train conductor hat that resembles a cross between The Rockettes Toy Soldier costumes and English bearskin caps.

Transforming is exactly the point: “Vaquera has always celebrated fashion’s transformative power,” read Vaquera’s show notes. “The collection confronts the tension between perfection and chaos. Can you be unhinged and complete at once? Its cast of characters—distorted drab mods, twisted ladies who lunch, abstracted leather daddies—all seem to suggest that the most covetable clothes for your future are those that mirror our fractured present.”

While years of the past were defined by singular aesthetics, 2026 lacks one solo homogeneous style. Formality, too, has been traded for casual looks. Hats used to be ubiquitous; now they’re sort of a rare dying breed, save for a baseball cap.

Perhaps that’s one of the reasons why these character-driven hats are so prevalent now. Many of them are tied to uniforms, occupations, or the everyday made extreme. It’s beautiful absurdism, verging on delightfully unhinged. Consider an over-the-top hat pure whimsy.

#6814. 12 Things You Should Toss From Your Kitchen ASAP Before Thanksgiving

Experts say a quick kitchen edit now can save holiday stress later.

It’ll soon be the most important day of the year in the kitchen, so give yourself the gift of space and freedom from clutter by doing a quick purge.

“Thanksgiving needs every inch of counter, fridge, and cabinet space you’ve got,” says Ann Lightfoot, cofounder of DDH Home Organizing & Move Management. “A short edit beforehand means you can find the baster when you need it, the leftovers have somewhere to go, and you aren’t digging past three broken whisks to reach a serving spoon.”

But don’t overdo it! “You don’t need a Pinterest-perfect pantry. You need room to work,” says Lightfoot. “A full organizing project can easily turn into a weekend of half-finished bins, and that’s the last thing anyone needs in November.”

Instead of tearing apart the entire kitchen, focus on the areas and items that will have the most impact. “We always say edit before you organize, and this is the editing part: take things out,” says Lightfoot. “Do one quick pass, ask whether each item earns its space, and let the rest go. Labels and matching containers can wait until January.”

Ahead, here’s what experts say to get rid of ASAP so your kitchen will be ready for cooking and entertaining at Thanksgiving.

“Spices lose their flavor over time, and stale cinnamon or a two-year-old jar of sage will make itself known in your pie and stuffing,” says Lightfoot. “Check the dates on baking soda, baking powder, and flour too. Toss what’s past its prime and make a shopping list while you’re at it.”

Glasses with scratches just don’t look great. “I'm all for mixing vintage and contemporary pieces, but damaged drinking glasses and dishes should go,” says Kerrie Kelly, NKBA, FASID, CEO and creative director of Kerrie Kelly Studio, and NKBA 2026 National Board Chair. “Holiday entertaining is a wonderful excuse to take inventory and make sure you have enough functional pieces for your guests.”

“Three napkins and a stack of faded plates won't set a beautiful table. Let them go and start fresh,” says Nikki Boyd, organizing expert, author of Beautifully Organized, and founder of At Home With Nikki.

It’s amazing how stuff gets pushed to the back of the fridge, never to be seen again. “Fridge space is prime real estate on Thanksgiving, between the turkey, the sides, and everything guests bring,” says Lightfoot. “Clear out the half-empty dressings, the jam from last summer, and anything you can’t identify.”

Be honest with yourself. “If it hasn't come out for a single holiday in years, it's not waiting for this one,” says Boyd. “Keep heirlooms with stories, and release the rest.”

“Kitchen drawers have a way of collecting multiples of things we rarely need more than one of,” says Laura Kinsella, founder of Urban OrgaNYze. “Pull out your spatulas, peelers, measuring cups, and all those cooking tools that always seem to get stuck in the drawer. If you're not reaching for them when you're hosting 20 people, chances are you don't need them for a regular weeknight dinner either.”

“Your table is your stage. Burnt down candles and stained runners don't belong on it,” says Boyd.

Containers that have no lids need to go away ASAP. Ditto for lids that don’t have a container. “Before the holiday leftovers start piling up, take 10 minutes to match your food storage containers with their lids. Get rid of anything that's cracked, warped, or missing its match,” says Kinsella. “There's nothing more frustrating than having a refrigerator full of leftovers and realizing you can't find a single lid that fits!”

That bread maker you haven’t touched lately? The air fryer that’s collecting dust? It’s time to donate them. “Any big kitchenware item that you haven’t used for the past two to three holiday seasons needs to go,” says Amelia Meena, owner of Appleshine, Organization + Design.

If they’re in bad shape, treat yourself to some new ones. “Nonstick pans with a flaking coating and sheet pans warped beyond saving make cooking harder than it has to be,” says Lightfoot. “If you’ve been meaning to replace one, do it now so you aren’t stuck mid-recipe.”

Soy sauce and ketchup packets, plastic forks, extra napkins, and the stack of menus add up quickly. You’ll want that drawer space for foil, twine, and the meat thermometer, so toss the whole lot into the garbage immediately, says Lightfoot.

Stained, threadbare towels and thin pot holders aren’t safe for pulling a hot roasting pan out of the oven—plus, raggedy mitts don’t exactly scream “festive.” Pitch thin pot holders and recycle old towels into cleaning rags, then treat yourself to a cute new set of kitchen linens, says Lightfoot.

#6812. You Don’t Need Designer Sneakers. You Need These $95 German Army Trainers.

We must admit that these ones from Quince are damn good.

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

Welcome to the Esquire Endorsement. Heavily researched. Thoroughly vetted. These picks are the best way to spend your hard-earned cash.

In my life, I lean toward luxury and secondhand clothing wherever possible, desperately trying to get away from all the cheap garbage being sold to me on Instagram ads and the Amazon homepage. I’ve spent years of my life hunting sales and eBay listings for clothes and boots. I’m like an edge-habitat pine growing in the direction of the radiant sun that is well-made clothing, trying to forget the fast fashion slop that lies in the forest behind me.

But I throw that out the window when it comes to sneakers. Designer sneakers are, for me, one of the dumbest things I could ever buy. Even when they are made with real leather, you are paying for a plastic sole that has a lifespan of a few years. I don’t think you should pay more than the $200 price of a pair of New Balance when it comes to sneakers.

Under that price point, I’ve never been able to find a good pair German Army Trainers, which I have always wanted. That changed when I found these. Quince (yeah yeah, I was just complaining about fashion slop, but life is full of contradictions) makes a perfect pair of GATs—and it makes them for $95. I honestly think every man in the world should buy a pair of these.

This is my real qualm with designer sneakers, and it totally undercuts anything you could tell me about the second-hand sneaker hype market. What you should pay for, when you pay expensive prices for clothing, is craftsmanship. When you buy a Gucci 1953 loafer or Loro Piana cashmere you probably arrived there because of the brand, but you are paying for the craftsmanship. I see no such correlation in designer sneakers, even the ones those brands make.

But a $95 pair of kicks? That’s honest. Even though I’m not bullish on Quince’s fast fashion take on quiet luxury (nor am I bullish on its caviar program), and the fact that Quince chose to closely replicate the Margiela GAT instead of the original German army models, I will let it slide. At $95, there are no claims being made about leather quality, or the footbed, or whatever is going on in the sole you can’t see. They look good and are easy to replace; it’s about as honest of a deal as you can find shopping these days.

The thing about the original BW Sport GATs—which you can get for about this price still, though used workout sneakers aren’t my cup of tea—is that they’re just about bulletproof. Those original mid-century designs made were first issued in the 1970s and stopped being issued around the end of the Cold War, a real feat of durability.

These shoes mimic that Army-issued durability. I’ve worn these sneakers for going on a year now. In that time, I’ve seen many pairs of more expensive kicks start to fall apart, get scuffed beyond recognition, and stink like hell. These have not. The pair I’ve worn all year is the pair pictured in this story. Nothing I say in this endorsement could be more convincing than that.

And really that’s the argument here. When I wrote about the Chuck Taylors I normally wear, it was a use-it-and-lose-it argument—they cost $45, who cares if the soles get holes within 12 months. But here, I fear I’m going to sound like a marketing mouthpiece for Quince. These shoes are $95, but they’ll last just as long as a pair that cost you $950. That’s all you can ask for these days.

#6809. The Art of the Winter Layer

Use these cold-weather staples from The North Face for practical warmth with polished style.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Like any specialized skill set, winter layering is one that must be continually practiced and perfected, lest your talents wane. It’s not as easy as throwing on a pair of cashmere leggings and a coordinating hoodie—that’s only the beginning. From there, it takes a careful curation of hero pieces (like puffer jackets and parkas), as well as a cast of supporting details (hats, gloves, and high-performance footwear), to layer effectively and aesthetically in the harshest conditions.

That said, even the most adept artist is nothing without an arsenal of trusted creative tools. And in these bitter temps, you’ll want to reach for the best, which essentially means any piece of gear with The North Face’s iconic rectangular logo attached to it. The storied brand has dominated the outdoor space for decades, having perfected the art of elevated style at elevated altitudes.

As we head into the chilliest season of the year, look to The North Face’s vast selection of dependable staples for all your layering needs. Designed both for performance and appearances, these pieces are in it for the long run.

Whether painting or dressing, it’s essential to start any creative endeavor with a blank canvas made of quality materials. A good base should be versatile and simple to pair with a host of helpful staples. Long-sleeve tees, cashmere turtlenecks, and crewneck sweatshirts, for example, are all good jumping-off points.

If you’re looking for a high-performance piece with enough style power to stand on its own, we recommend the Women’s Chabot 2.0 Mock-Neck. This cozy layering top offers the same reliable comfort of a traditional insulated thermal with a few modern updates. Though understated by design, its delightfully oversized fit and a funky waffle knit texture make the basic feel intentional and interesting.

For a closer-fitting base, the Women’s Golden Ridge Ribbed Long-Sleeve Tee layers easily under other pieces. Its slim fit and ribbed texture give this practical layer a polished look, while thumbholes at the cuffs add a functional detail. Bonus points for the tee’s anti-odor technology that helps keep the fabric feeling fresh.

Women’s Golden Ridge Ribbed Long-Sleeve Tee

After you’ve selected the first layer, the next stop should be your coat closet. This is where you’ll select the hero of your look. While each piece of the layering puzzle is uniquely important, the power jacket is a non-negotiable. The right iteration should supply a thick layer of warmth, while also doing its part to make the outfit, as a whole, feel cohesive.

Those who crave a more subdued winter aesthetic will love the classic appeal of the Women’s Arctic Bomber. The waterproof winter jacket boasts all the utility of a parka, with the sleek design details most commonly found in trend-focused outerwear. In four comforting colorways, this winter coat is an insulation powerhouse in a chic, wearable package.

Look to the Women’s Hydrenalite Down Jacket for a more classic puffer. This workhorse is a versatile down layer that can be slipped on at any time to keep you warm for any duration that you spend outdoors, whether you are on the mountain or running around town.

For the more artistically inclined, try the Women’s Yumiori Off Peak Full Zip Jacket. This fleece outer layer offers unfailing warmth and a distinctly sporty flavor. Its two-tone color palette, meanwhile, adds a fun, whimsical feel to the utilitarian, zip-up-style silhouette.

During the summer months, it’s all about the mani-pedi. But once that icy weather blows in, self-care starts to look a bit different. The North Face’s Etip Gloves are basically a hand treatment on the go. Crafted from soft, stretchy fleece made with 93 percent recycled polyester, these tech-friendly gloves will keep your hands comfortable on cold-weather outings. They’ll also keep you connected: Touchscreen compatibility lets you check your phone without taking them off, while silicone grip dots on the palms help you hold onto your device as well as smaller essentials like keys and credit cards.

For footwear, the Women’s THERMOBALL Traction Mule V will quickly become the standout of your seasonal lineup. These cloud-like slip-ons pair warm insulation with a quilted upper that gives them a casual, streetwear-cool vibe. The rubber outsole adds traction for quick trips outdoors.

The minimalist philosophy requires you to take off one item before leaving the house. But during the cold weather season, it’s in your best interest to do the opposite. As you walk out the door, make sure you grab a beanie since most of your body heat can escape from your head.

Beanies are simultaneously the most underappreciated outfit addition and the most indispensable. The North Face’s Wool Blend Beanie, for instance, pairs the warmth of its 65 percent merino wool knit with a refined, metropolitan style. Its classic cuffed design and textured knit add visual interest, while its deep fit offers roomier coverage. If you prefer the rectangular logo with the same cuffed look, you can never go wrong with the rib-knit and soft lining of the Salty Lined Beanie. On the slopes or on your morning commute, either will add a polished finishing touch.

The importance of a functional winter hat cannot be overstated—think of it as the final brushstroke in the art of winter layering.

#6806. 9 Interior Trends Designers Are Officially Ditching in 2027

Some of this year’s biggest design moments may not age well.

The end of the year is a great time to look back and reflect. When it comes to home design, there’s a lot to cover, from new trends to furniture collaboration drops to specific internet-breaking interiors. One of our favorite things to do around this time is figure out what’s coming next in terms of interiors.

We love predicting what’s going to be hot in home design for the upcoming seasons; however, you can’t talk about what’s going to be “in” without also touching on what’s going to be “out.” We asked a handful of designers to share what design choices and interior trends they saw a lot of in 2026 that they’re more than happy to leave behind in 2027. Keep reading to find out the nine things they said.

We spend so much time making our interiors warm and reflective of our personalities, it would be a shame to ruin the look of these spaces by opting for one-dimensional lighting.

“It's time to move beyond relying on a single overhead fixture or wall-to-wall recessed lighting to illuminate an entire room,” designer Kristen Mendoza of Four Brothers Design + Build says. “Flat, overly bright lighting can make even the most beautifully designed spaces feel sterile and uninviting.”

Instead, incorporating layers of lighting to add dimension and create a warm atmosphere is much better for your home. Sconces, picture lights, table lamps, and thoughtfully placed accent lighting at various heights throughout the room, Mendoza adds, give a space a more intimate touch.

“I also recommend using warm 2700K light sources on dimmers to flatter people, highlight architectural details, and bring out the natural beauty of materials,” she explains. “Lighting should be considered early in the design and construction process, not treated as an afterthought.”

Part of the appeal of “grandma chic” decor is that it’s been collected over time. The pieces show their age, the interior is imperfect, and it’s very clearly reflective of the homeowner’s personality and life. However, “there is a difference between a room that feels ‘collected over time’ and one that feels inherited all at once,” designer Stephanie Kraus explains, and she’s tired of seeing this false presentation on display in people’s homes.

“Heavy Roman shades with lots of fabric, chintz on top of chintz on top of chintz, fringe on every edge, etc.,” she adds. “One of these details in a room can be charming, but if you use them all together, the room can start to feel like a period movie set.”

It’s often clear when this eccentric aesthetic is manufactured rather than effortless. Instead of trying to make the “ideal” interior in the span of a month, be patient and work on your home over a greater span of time. That way, the end product will look authentic.

Though curved sofas are massively popular right now and look gorgeous in a photograph, Kraus is ready to leave them in 2026. “A curved sofa rarely seats more than two people comfortably,” she says. “Once guests settle in, everyone ends up sitting awkwardly, and conversation feels harder than it should.”

She’s all for a sofa or couch being something that invites people in to linger over conversations and stay late into the night, and a kidney-shaped seat isn’t going to do that.

While designer Maggie Vollrath of Provision Studios loved seeing the return of decorative, playful details like ruffles and scalloped edges, she thinks we’ve gone a bit overboard in 2026. These touches are being applied to just about everything: upholstery, pillows, lampshades, bedding, furniture—the list could go on.

“These details can be incredibly charming, but when they're repeated throughout an entire room, they begin to lose the very character that makes them special,” she says.

Rather than treat every piece of a room with one of these details, Vollrath suggests opting for a scalloped lampshade or a beautifully tailored ruffled pillow instead to still capture that charm without drowning the space in them.

“Limiting these details to one or two thoughtful applications allows them to feel intentional rather than overly thematic,” she adds. “Sometimes, the most interesting interiors are as much about what you choose to leave out as what you include.”

“I'd love to see us move away from selecting materials simply because they imitate the appearance of something more expensive,” Vollrath explains. This goes beyond marble-printed contact paper and burl wood veneer; the designer means on a larger scale, like mass-produced tile that’s made to replicate the imperfections of handmade zellige.

“Part of what makes authentic zellige so beautiful is the craftsmanship and natural variation that comes from its production,” she says. “When those qualities are artificially reproduced, I think we sometimes lose the very thing that made the original material special.”

She would rather see a greater appreciation for beautiful, honest materials at every price point, and if the exact thing a homeowner wants is out of budget, then her solution would be to pivot the idea altogether rather than find something cheaply made that looks like what they desire.

“A classic Carrara marble paired with beautifully considered cabinetry can create an incredibly sophisticated interior, even when something as dramatic as Calacatta Viola isn't within the budget,” Vollrath explains.

We could probably say this every year, but it bears repeating: Don’t solely follow trends! “Just because something is trending doesn't mean it's right for your home,” designer Drew Michael Scott of Lone Fox says. “Polka dots are having a moment right now, but they don't make sense in many homes, or dare I say, most homes.”

He suggests thinking of home trends as prompts that should get you to brainstorm new ideas for your space that actually fit your style. Take polka dots again. If you want to introduce a new pattern to your home, but you don’t particularly mesh with polka dots, try a stripe instead.

“If you try to force something you don't love into your home just because it's trending, you're going to drive yourself crazy,” he adds. Let’s leave this line of thinking back in 2026 once and for all.

While we love a good built-in bookshelf and wooden ceiling beam, those types of architectural details don’t always make sense in every single home. In 2026, as personality-filled interiors became more popular for everyone, a lot of homeowners looked into adding this type of millwork to their spaces as a way to add more visual interest and texture.

“Decorative beams, arches, and elaborate millwork can feel forced when they don't make sense with the architecture of the home,” designer Dani Flax of Pearson Design Group argues. “I think there's a tendency to add these elements to make a space feel more interesting, but the result can actually take away from the architecture itself.”

A home in a modern farmhouse style, for example, would look a bit odd with an intricate ceiling medallion and excessive picture frame molding. Design your interior around the existing architecture and the style of your home, don’t incorporate these elements simply because they’re everywhere right now.

The next year is not about playing it safe with your interiors—designers are tired of the stark white home. While ubiquitous gray and white color schemes had their time, they can often make a home feel generic and devoid of character.

“In their place, we're embracing more intentional, tonal palettes and color drenching,” Mendoza says.

You can still have a mostly white house, of course, but take a little risk and mix in some pops of color and pattern here and there, or choose a beautiful neutral wood tone for your cabinetry instead of a bright white paint.

“Taking a considered color, whether it's a deep green, warm clay, or earthy mushroom, and carrying it across walls, trim, and cabinetry creates a cohesive, enveloping effect,” Mendoza adds. “The goal isn't necessarily to introduce more color, but to use it with greater confidence and purpose.”

This is definitely a hot take, but designer John Maloney McNamara of Coosa Interiors is ready to leave velvet upholstery behind. “I’ve tried, but velvet almost always reads as either a 1990s prom limo or a hotel lobby trying very hard,” he explains. “The sheen shows every crush and bruise, and it ages into something that looks tired rather than loved.”

If you love the look of velvet, he suggests going with a mohair fabric instead, saying it has all of velvet’s depth and none of its shine. It also only gets better with age. And though he knows creamy bouclé has been overdone, Maloney McNamara thinks it deserves a reprise, but only in a rich color that can replace velvet still.

#6801. Dancing with the Stars Judge Carrie Ann Inaba on the ‘Healing’ Power of Movement and Why She Takes Risks

In ELLE’s Office Hours series, we ask people in powerful positions about their first jobs, worst jobs, and everything in between. This month, we sat down with Dancing with the Stars judge and dancer Carrie Ann Inaba. For the uninitiated, Inaba has been the sole female judge on the hit dance competition show since its inception, but her ambitions in entertainment began long before she arrived in the ballroom. After being discovered at a talent show in Hawaii, Inaba moved to Japan to pursue her dreams of performing, a leap of faith that catapulted her career to new heights. From choreographing and staging shows like American Idol and So You Think You Can Dance to bringing ballroom dance into the homes of millions, her career has been full of big risks and what she calls the “healing art” of dance. Ahead of the season 35 finale of Dancing with the Stars, Inaba reflects on how she got her start in the biz and the moment that changed everything in her career, then pulls back the curtain on what makes Dancing with the Stars a true feat of live television.

My very first job was working for my father when I was about 10 or 11 years old. He was an entrepreneur and, at the time, a real estate developer with an office in the heart of Waikiki. After school or on weekends, I would go to his office, and he would always put me to work. I think those early experiences are why I’ve always had such a positive association with work.

I was “discovered” by a Japanese producer at a talent show in Hawaii called Search for Talent. I was dancing with my friend Tina Horii, and we were offered a recording contract with Pony Canyon Records, with the intention of eventually returning to the U.S. as crossover artists. At the last moment, she decided not to go, but I felt compelled to honor the commitment. As part of my recording deal, I negotiated a contract to perform as a dancer on one of Japan’s most popular television shows, Yoru no Hit Studio DX. My love of dancing was still my first priority. I loved that chapter of my life. I was a member of the Dancing Dolls, much like the Solid Gold Dancers or the troupe on Dancing with the Stars. We performed alongside the musical guests, and it was a dream come true. My recording career was more challenging. I was uncomfortable being the center of attention, and everything felt rushed. It felt more like a business than a creative endeavor. The day after I performed my first single, “Party Girl,” on Fuji TV, I was mobbed by fans in Harajuku. It was an incredible introduction to the world of live television, which has become a thread throughout my career.

When I booked Dancing with the Stars, suddenly an entirely new world of opportunities opened up to me, and I wasn’t necessarily ready for all of them. Until then, I had been very intentional about the direction of my career. I was focused on dance, choreography, and producing. Everything had dance at its center. I had produced some live shows but really wanted to produce television. So the job of judging on Dancing with the Stars felt like a good fit toward that goal. What [the show] gave me was the opportunity to learn my own voice.

At 18, I moved to Japan, a country where I didn’t speak the language. I asked to be released from my recording contract when I realized the direction of my career was no longer aligned with who I was. I’ve never been afraid to walk away from an opportunity when staying would mean compromising my values.

Later, I chose to accept the job of opening Madonna’s Girlie Show Tour by doing something that had never been done before: descending a 50-foot unsecured fire pole with a non-weight-bearing safety. It was basically a live stunt that I performed every night of that tour. I had to go through intense training for it. It was controversial, but I really liked the idea of it and the statement it was making, so I said yes. It was one of the scariest things I’ve ever done; there was real risk every time I got on that pole. But it was very rewarding and I believed in what I was doing. As an Asian American woman, I wanted to break down stereotypes of what we could do.

I also think I made a very bold move this year by standing up for myself amid some workplace drama. I’m still processing what happened, and since the competition is still going on, I will leave it at that. But it was a profound moment for me in my career and life.

To trust myself, trust my choices, and always speak my truth no matter how uncomfortable it is to do so. I live by that.

It’s so much more than just steps and technique—it is a healing art form that empowers people. I encourage and notice the aspects outside and around the technique because that is what I know to be important from my personal and professional experiences. After a dance is done, most people will not remember the steps themselves or how many heel leads they had or didn’t have; they will remember how the dance made them feel. Of course, they need to do the correct style we have asked of them and follow any rules we have established, but we aren’t creating professional dancers to compete in Blackpool. We are an entertainment show that really celebrates the human spirit and the courage to try something new. That is what makes our show so special.

I can personally say that in 35 seasons, I have never been told what score to give a performance. Not once. I don’t think I would be able to continue judging if that were ever to happen. It would go against my core values and everything I believe about the responsibility of being a judge.

I don’t think people fully understand the scope of what we accomplish each week. The sheer amount of creative and physical energy it takes to bring this show to life is extraordinary. Every week, we essentially make the impossible possible. From choreography, performance, production, storytelling, and costume design to social media strategy, brand partnerships, publicity, security, catering, and transportation, there are so many moving parts. And once we start that first episode, it never stops until the Tuesday before Thanksgiving. It’s a feat on its own, but it’s also that we do it live every week.

There are no do-overs. Live television is high-stakes and high-pressure, and Dancing with the Stars is unlike anything else on television. The production is so elaborate that I sometimes wonder if people realize it’s all unfolding in real time.

It’s an honor to work on a show that is as demanding as it is fulfilling. We create compelling television that brings people together. People throw watch parties, and families across generations have something they can enjoy and talk about together. In a world where it’s increasingly easy to become isolated in our own individual experiences, Dancing with the Stars gives us a shared moment.

For this finale, viewers on both coasts will have the opportunity to watch and vote live, making that shared experience even more special.

When a dance transcends the steps, the technique, and the choreography, and somehow becomes greater than the sum of its parts, that’s the magic that makes it a ten for me. I can feel it. And that magic is what keeps bringing me back season after season.

#6799. 6 Stylish Ways Designers Make Vintage Tile the Star of the Room

Here’s how to give this charming, old-school detail new life.

When we redesign, remodel, and renovate, it can be tempting to update, replace, and modernize every nook and cranny of your home. But the goal is rarely to chase newness. It’s easy to see vintage details, like quirky tile, as an obstacle standing between your home and a modern look, but tearing it out might make your heart ache later.

“I love the irregularities you find in older tiles, whether it's subtle variations in color, an imperfect glaze, or the undulation of a tile's surface. Those imperfections are what make them so beautiful, giving a room texture, character, and a sense of craftsmanship,” says Ali Burgoon Nolan, founder and principal designer at Studio Burgoon. Tile is one of the vintage details homeowners regret removing the most, as modern-day designs and materials lack the panache, durability, and craftsmanship of decades past. Not to mention, the removal and reinstallation will cost you a big chunk of your budget.

“Just like in other areas of the home, introducing a vintage element helps to create more interesting, storied spaces,” says Johanna Lyle, founder of Jo Lyle & Co. “When we mix elements from different eras, the home feels more unique and collected over time. If you've bought an old home and aren't sure you love the existing, perhaps historic, tile, try to change some things around it before you give up on it completely. You might not dig it just because you haven't seen it before, or it's not what is currently popular.”

If you’re lucky enough to have inherited vintage tile in your historic home, here are six ways designers have given it the main character energy it deserves.

Jennie Bishop preserved the charm of this century-old Illinois foyer by buffing the shine back into the home’s original tile. Her team then refinished the adjacent wood staircase and painted the walls a creamy white to brighten the room.

Designer Galena Younger knows potential when she sees it, and this historic cottage in San Antonio was no exception. The home’s original Mexican-style tiles surround the living room hearth, complemented by family heirlooms scattered around the room for an ultrapersonal, deliciously vintage aesthetic.

Interior and jewelry designer Trish Becker preserved this home’s original tile mantel, using it as the starting point for the room’s design. A corn-husk woven rug adds earthy warmth, while touches of green connect the room’s architectural details to its bold patterned slipper chairs.

With the goal of restoring her home’s “1931 glory,” designer Claire Thomas was ecstatic to find this bathroom’s original purple untouched, despite many renovations by previous owners. Playing on the hue, she brought in soft floral wallpaper and skirted purple stools for a feminine edge, finishing the room with a sage vanity for a pop of color and soft contrast.

Artist Dana Gibson and interior designer Sara Hillery brought a playful touch to this sunroom, keeping the home’s original tile floors as the foundation. They drew out the tiles’ blue tones in the plush textiles, then added woven furniture to complement its earthy browns.

It doesn’t get more classic than a black-and-white design scheme. In this Richmond bath, Gibson and Hillery leaned into the existing retro tiles, opting to carry the palette through the room’s entire design.

#6789. Omega and Swatch Just Launched a New MoonSwatch—and No Two Are the Same

The Mission to Earthphase – Silver Snowflake, the 39th watch in the series, will have collectors keeping an eye on the Swiss weather forecast.

By MoonSwatch standards, it’s been a quiet year. Swatch has been otherwise occupied with the Audemars Piguet Royal Pop, the May release for which people lined up for six days in New York, police deployed tear gas in France, and which, according to Swatch Group, has generated more than 25 billion views on social media.

Not that interest in the MoonSwatch has gone away.

An estimated 4.5 million have been sold since the collaboration began in March 2022 (and that figure only takes us to the end of 2024). In July this year, some 1.2 million people applied to buy one of the 1,969 examples of its $570 Mission to the Moon 1969, a watch that incorporated 11 grams of 18-carat gold recycled from vintage Omega components.

The latest MoonSwatch—only the third new model this year, compared with 11 in 2023—is the Mission to Earthphase – Silver Snowflake.

An all-black counterpart to last winter’s all-white Cold Moon edition, it takes as its starting point the idea that no two snowflakes are alike.

Swatch has developed a digital process capable of generating millions of different snowflake patterns, one of which is laser-engraved onto the moonphase indicator of each watch. So, unusually for a mass-produced quartz watch, every example is unique.

It also features the complication Swatch introduced in November 2024 and which remains exclusive to the MoonSwatch: an earthphase indicator. Where a conventional moonphase shows the phases of the Moon as viewed from Earth, this does the reverse. The two displays run in opposite directions over the same 29.5-day cycle.

(How useful this is to those of us who live on Earth is debatable, but it’s one of the more original ideas in watchmaking in recent years.)

There are some nice details elsewhere on the 42mm Bioceramic watch, including Snoopy and Woodstock in the snow, a pair of miniature skis at 11 o’clock, and a tiny patch of white on the Earth representing a snow-covered Switzerland, which glows green under UV light.

As with last year’s winter edition, there’s a stipulation.

The watch goes on sale at selected Swatch stores worldwide on Black Friday, November 27. After that, until March 20, 2027, the last day of winter, you’ll only be able to buy one when it’s snowing in Switzerland.

Swatch will be providing weather updates on its website.

#6788. 50 White Elephant Gifts Under $50 That Are Practically Guaranteed to Be Stolen

Every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Beware, these picks might start some fights.

I’ve been writing gift guides as a shopping editor for years. Usually, I’m very sentimental, wanting to recommend thoughtful gifts to make your loved ones smile. But all bets are off when it comes to White Elephant gifts. I want to cause chaos at your family gift swap. Your gift should be the one everyone fights over.

If you're not sure what a White Elephant exchange is or how it works, just know this: it's really fun, and it's one of the only times when stealing is not only totally acceptable, but encouraged. Basically, it's a blind gift exchange that, when the recipient reveals the gift they chose, they can keep it or put it back and steal someone else's gift. It's a cheeky little game that is a great way to get into the holiday spirit.

It’s also a really affordable way to exchange gifts as a big group. No worries about finding the perfect thing for someone specific. Just bring something cool enough for anybody to enjoy, and there’s usually a budget cap. So for this guide, I provided the best white elephant gifts under $50. They’re so budget-friendly and unique that you might want to do all of your gift shopping below, or buy some items of your own. Worry not; we won’t judge.

This is the ultimate tool for any candle lover. In just one sleek, swan-shaped package, it’s a candle snuffer, wick dipper, trimmer, and wax spoon. It comes in gold or raven black, and it’ll be perfect coffee table decor.

Time to level up that holiday hot cocoa. This spice kit comes with the classic velvety cocoa mix, in addition to sustainably harvested Guntur Sannam chili and fragrant cardamom pods. Your hot chocolate can be as complex as your morning cup of chai.

No city-dweller will say no to extra storage. It’s especially helpful when it comes in a cute and colorful package, like these cache boxes. Use it to hide junk mail, Q-tips, or any other tiny clutter.

The plant lover in your life will jump at the chance to steal this care essential. The GOHA Leaf Sweep is Associate Shopping Editor Janae McKenzie’s secret to a shiny, eye-catching houseplant collection. “I use it to clean my plant’s broad leaves, especially the tall ones out of reach,” McKenzie says. “It prevents dirt buildup and keeps pests at bay.” We even have a special code for HB readers to save 10% on this handy tool: use HB10 at checkout.

Yes, they might own a wine opener already, but we doubt it’s as cute as this corkscrew. The color-blocked bow tie shape makes opening the next bottle look even more fun. A bar cart isn’t complete without it.

#6785. The 6 Best Gaming Headsets for All Types of Players

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

Whether you’re playing single-player or online, these will level up your game.

Nothing truly makes me feel immersed in a game the same way good sound does. And it’s impossible to get that level of tension in a horror game like Resident Evil, or the feeling of being absolutely locked in a competitive shooter without a good pair of headphones. Nowadays, video games are fully open world of 3D and spatial audio, and there's never been a better time to hop on the bandwagon. It's time to get a gaming headset.

If you consider gaming your main hobby, you’re probably either a single-player person or you like to squad up in your battle royale of choice. It doesn’t matter, actually, because the only proper way to experience both ends of the gaming spectrum is with a headset. For single-player, that means fully immersive audio. For multiplayer, you’ll sound crystal clear to your teammates—no more confusion or excuses. The good noise-canceling headsets even have transparency modes so you don’t have to ignore everyone in your real life either.

Here's the problem. There are actually plenty of good headsets and trustworthy brands that make dozens of similar options. Finding the headset that will work for you isn’t made to be easy, but that’s why I’m here. I know my gaming headsets like the back of my hand—that’s my job. To figure out if you need a high-end wireless SteelSeries headset, or if you’ll be happy with a sub-$100 option, read on. Hell, maybe you’d prefer earbuds. I’ve accounted for all options.

This is the one gaming headset I won’t (and frankly can’t) say anything negative about. I suppose that’s what $600 gets you. SteelSeries has long made comfortable headsets that support multiple platforms with easy swapping. It introduced the world to its GameHub base station, letting you connect all your systems to one panel and easily control them all from there.

The Nova Elite takes every already perfectly solved puzzle piece and puts a little extra sheen on it. First off, it is gorgeous, with exteriors made from premium steel, aluminum, and vegan leather. Nothing else in the gaming space compares to it in terms of the luxe look. In terms of fit, the Nova Elite distributes its weight evenly so you can play for hours without discomfort.

And this headset’s gaming hub has an extra feature that really changes things. The hot-swappable batteries are SteelSeries’ biggest innovation in recent years, and here the hub also acts as a charger for your second (included) headset battery. So whichever one is not powering your current session is being charged. What this means is battery life is a solved problem. You literally never have to worry about running out of charge mid-game again. And for some, that alone might be worth the price of admission.

Okay, forget what I just said. This is everything a wireless headset needs to be for the average gamer. ASUS has targeted a lower price point and succeeded in terms of knowing which features to cut, and what to keep to make it still feel like a high-quality experience. You don't get active noise cancellation or the ability to play audio from two sources at once. For those luxuries, go for the Delta II.

At 0.7 pounds, the Pelta is remarkably light and the furthest thing from bulky. It's about letting you play all day on those summer Saturdays where it's too hot to go outside. Where it surprises in this regard is battery life. Offering up to 70 hours between charges and a fit that won't leave you itchy and sweaty, this is the all-nighter-friendly headset.

While I wouldn't personally spring for a wired headset, those who do are hard to convince otherwise. And that crowd has spent the last couple of years rallying around the HyperX Cloud Alpha. If competitive gaming is the reason you are turning to a headset, this has everything you need for under $100.

You aren't going to get the audio options you do from the multi-hundred-dollar headsets SteelSeries and Corsair sell. Instead, you are paying a reasonable price for a high-quality microphone, and a comfortable pair of headphones. Stop worrying about lag and stop worrying about your headset running out of battery. It's time to wire in.

When it comes to sound quality, the Corsair Virtuoso Max brings it to a new level. This is a better-sounding headset than most of the readers of this article have ever experienced.

My favorite high-tech touch that we actually use is the simultaneous connection. Using the 2.4 GHz dongle and Bluetooth in tandem you can get the audio from your game and audio from a Bluetooth source at the same time. That means pumping in your own tunes or a background podcast while grinding levels. When playing with friends, I love the addition of a physical, sturdy, functional mic mute button.

The only issue is long-term comfort. Weighing in at just under a pound, the 60-hour battery life on the headset is a bit of a moot point. You'll want to take it off anyway because it can start to feel quite hard on your skull after a couple hours of white knuckle gaming.

If you have a single gaming machine and that console is a PS5, this is the headset I recommend. It is remarkably lightweight, weighing even less than the wired-only pair I recommended earlier, and it’s super easy to use—with a satisfying mute button that pops in and out, and a microphone that is entirely detachable. So if you’re settling in for a night of solo horror gaming, you can set the mic aside and still enjoy the excellent sound and spatial audio options. And if you know that battery is low, or you really just want the easiest solution, the package includes a 3.5mm cable for wired connection. Just plug that right into your DualSense controller and you’re off to the races.

Beyond just PlayStation diehards, this is an excellent option for any PC or Nintendo gamer who wants a light wireless headset. It is fully compatible via USB-C transceiver or headphone cable with any other modern console, sans the Xbox.

Okay, so I lied. When you clicked on this for the six best headsets, yeah one of these isn't a gaming headset at all. It's a set of earbuds designed by SteelSeries to be used on gaming consoles and it's as much of a game-changer as it sounds. If you feel cheated, don't fret. There are two more headsets listed in the honorable mentions below. Please accept my humble offering.

If you’ll allow me to talk about them for just a minute though, the Arctis GameBuds are just shy of a miracle. They are comfy earbuds with all-encompassing noise-canceling (gasp!), spatial audio support, and a very useful transparency/talk-through mode. The sound isn't quite on par with SteelSeries's larger headsets, but it still impresses. Plus, unlike the rest of these headsets, you can fit them in your pocket.

SteelSeries Arctis Nova 7 ($179): You don't need to shell out for the Nova Elite to get a good Arctis headset. This one uses a simple USB-C dongle, so isn't nearly as complicated to set up, either.

Turtle Beach Stealth Pro 2: ($349): My favorite new headset of the year. An excellent multi-platform choice with high-quality playback and call audio. It also uses a swappable battery system, so you never run out of charge in a heated gaming moment.

Testing gaming headsets really isn't too difficult. You make sure it's compatible with what it says on the box, and then tell the people if it’s comfortable and if it sounds good. Shit simple until you do it enough to realize a simple truth. Most models from reputable brands are worth their costs, and very few companies have duds in their lineups. That said, there are ways to tell what's going to rise from the crop. Here's some pointers for the next time you shop for headsets.

Comfort — If you can't stay comfortable in them for more than an hour they are going straight in the trash. Even the most uncomfortable among these picks are still in the top 5% of comfortable gaming headphones.

Sound Quality — Like with the pair of headphones you use to listen to music, you want clear sound with plenty of range.

Microphone — If you're gaming online, your microphone needs to cut out unwanted background noise. Some offer noise cancelling, some just have good unidirectional builds. All on this list are great in this department.

Directional Sound — Spatial audio is cool when watching movies, but when playing games this can take your team play to the next level. When you hear an enemy's footsteps, you can know they're behind you at four o'clock, not six. And that makes you an asset. It also makes the taste of victory that much sweeter.

Connection — I will discuss wireless vs. wired shortly, but when it comes to the going wireless there's usually two ways to connect a gaming headset. Bluetooth or via a USB dongle. The latter typically has less latency and is the preferred way to connect.

Are wired or wireless headsets better for gaming?

If you care about latency (aka lag), we are going to recommend wired over wireless. The added hassle of wireless charging and connecting doesn't necessarily make up for the hassle of having a wire. Plus, you don't have to worry about it not working on some devices—which you do with pretty much every wireless device you buy.

Do all gaming headsets work across all platforms?

I'm glad you asked. No! As you may have noticed, there tend to be two kinds of headsets. Those that work with Xbox.. and those that work with everything else. Since Xbox uses its own wireless standard instead of Bluetooth. In practice, this means Xbox gamers need to be extra careful when buying headsets to make sure the one they're getting is compatible. SteelSeries, for example, sells two versions of each headset, one marked for Xbox.

It's actually more complicated than "all headsets that work with PC also work with PlayStation and you have to get ones especially for Xbox," but in many of these cases that is the gist. Although the PlayStation headsets work on PC and Mac but not Nintendo Switch. So, yeah, it's pretty inconsistent. Seriously, just read the list of compatible platforms before you buy a headset.

#6783. Geri Halliwell’s New “Dark Honey” Hair Is Winter’s Most Expensive-Looking Color Trend: How to Recreate It

Rich, warm, and glossy, the Spice Girl’s new shade is winter-ready

Few hair colors are as iconic and instantly nostalgic as Geri Halliwell's natural red. The hue, synonymous with her nickname “Ginger Spice,” has, of course, evolved over the years, from copper highlights woven through fiery red lengths to a full head of golden blond and lighter strawberry-blond tones.

For winter, Halliwell has swapped her signature brighter tones for a richer shade. Enter dark honey hair. "What I absolutely love about Geri’s dark honey hair is the richness and depth of the color. A beautiful chestnut base with ribbons of warm honey, caramel, and subtle amber runs through the lengths and ends. It’s a wonderful evolution of her signature warmth, but with a softer, more understated finish," says celebrity hairstylist and Remi Cachet expert Adam Reed.

At the premiere of Only Murders in London, Halliwell wore her fresh hair color in a soft side part with dressed-out waves, a combination Reed says helps different tones catch the light.

The rich, luminous color adds subtle dimension that doesn't focus on dramatic placement, but on healthy-looking hair. "To recreate the look, I’d ask your colorist to maintain that beautiful brunette depth through the roots, introducing delicately placed honey and caramel lights through the mid-lengths and ends. A personalized gloss can bring those tones together and create that beautifully reflective finish," he adds.

Alternatively, Reed recommends his “just a little filler” approach, using extensions as color tools placed strategically. This approach uses additional hair to enhance color, density, and movement, rather than focusing solely on length. "By carefully selecting complementary shades of chestnut, honey, and caramel, we can introduce tonal variation without necessarily having to chemically lighten the natural hair," he notes.

Whether you're looking for a complete hair refresh this winter or simply want a subtle way to enhance your natural color without fully committing to a new look, Halliwell's dark honey hair is the perfect inspiration.

#6782. Inside a Layered Ski-in, Ski-out Retreat in the Mountains of Utah

An affectionate nickname inspired much of the design details.

Designers learn a lot of things about their clients when building or renovating their homes—it’s how they ensure the spaces actually feel like the homeowners. Their hobbies shape the purposes of distinct rooms, their tastes affect the color palette, and their experiences help to build out the decor. So, when designer McKenzie Matthews of Coven Haus (accidentally) learned that her client affectionately calls her husband The Wolf, she simply had to weave that part of their story into the design of their Park City, Utah, winter retreat.

“What started as a playful detail became a recurring theme, from a custom wolf head silhouette repeated along the secondary staircase to wolf hooks in the mudroom lockers,” Matthews says. The designer, who was part of the six-bedroom, seven-bathroom new-build from the start, wanted every aspect of the interior to feel like a luxurious and elevated boutique ski resort but with more personalized charm. “We carried the wolf motif into decorative pillows, artwork, and accessories, creating little moments of personality and meaning throughout the home.”

Outside of these smaller details, the rest of the ski-in, ski-out style home is layered with natural elements, like stone, reclaimed wood, and plaster, to complement the views outside of the Wasatch Mountain Range. The front door opens to a wood-clad foyer, topped with a vaulted ceiling accented with reclaimed wooden beams, which continues into the great room. Flanked by two double-sided stone fireplaces and looking out beyond the second floor of the deck into the woods, this gathering area invites any guest to escape the cold of the slopes and stay as long as they like.

Handmade and vintage pieces fill in any gaps, giving each room a collected feel. “One of my favorite examples is the primary bedroom bookcase, filled with unique objects and accessories we’ve gathered over the years,” Matthews says. “It’s those little details that give a home so much character.”

Spanning 11,758 square feet, it can be hard to make a house of this size truly feel homey, but Matthews’ dedication to the details ensured it was. “Every room has something special and unexpected, yet the entire home still feels cohesive,” she says. “I love that there's always something new to discover as you move through each space.”

FAST FACTSDesigner: McKenzie Matthews of Coven HausArchitect: Otto Walker Stylist: Lauren GastelumLocation: Park City, UtahThe Space: A six-bedroom, seven-bathroom ski-in, ski-out new build across 11,758 square feet.

The entry sets the tone for the rest of the home, with the wood-paneled walls, vaulted ceiling, limestone floor tile, and reclaimed beams serving as a warm, inviting escape from the cold outside. The variety of textures brings character and, along with the sculptural entry table, helps to soften the grand architectural details.

No detail is too small in this ski room. Marble knobs dot the top lockers, while a Calacatta Viola marble door jamb makes the mundane feel special. “With our clients being from Argentina, we wanted to do something a little unexpected and playful, starting with the textural floor tile,” Matthews says.

The fun continues to the ceiling, which is coated in the same red that lines the interior of the oak lockers, just in a matte finish. “We loved the idea of it feeling like a jewelry box,” the designer says of the painted locker interiors.

Fabric panels on the upper lockers soften the millwork and break up the oak, as does the painted boot wall which opens to the ski patio. “There are so many little details in this room, and I love every one of them!” Matthews adds.

Laying out the great room was a bit of a challenge. Flanked by two double-sided stone fireplaces, Matthews wanted to take advantage of the hearths without blocking or sacrificing the incredible view. “We opted for movable seating that could easily shift depending on how the space is used, while keeping the view as the star of the room,” she explains. The tumbleweed chandelier was the cherry on top, creating a bit of unexpected fun while bringing in an organic element.

To the right of the living room, beyond the fireplace, is a gaming corner, slightly blocked away from the main area in case any matches get a bit rowdy.

Downstairs in the living room, Matthews wanted plenty of seating for family and friends to gather, so they ordered a custom sectional with extra-deep seat cushions that comfortably seats at least eight people, if not more. “The reclaimed wood ceiling and exposed beams add so much warmth and character, while the soft furnishings keep the space feeling relaxed and lived in,” she adds.

If the family still has energy after a day skiing, they can always bond over a game of poker. Rich dark cocoa millwork and light-blocking drapery close off this space from the rest of the house, while the wall of books gives it character and ensures it still feels homey. If poker isn’t the game of choice, the wood top is removable so it doubles as a regular gaming or puzzle table.

“This might be my favorite room in the house,” Matthews says. “The ideas just kept flowing, and we reworked the bar layout a handful of times before landing here.” While the entire setup would make the most seasoned bartender jealous, it’s the details—like the patinated brass island, the tiled ceiling, the double bullnose countertop edge, and necklace-like sculptural chandelier—that makes the space a moment. “A little five-star resort experience without ever leaving home.”

Because Matthews’s clients wanted a dirty kitchen and a main one for entertaining, the designer could be a bit more creative here, choosing the finishes and features more for the way they look rather than how well they function. A calming blue and brown color palette makes it the most enticing spot for a quiet morning coffee or for setting out a grand buffet for party guests.

Since this is where all the cooking happens, functionality was Matthews’s biggest priority, from the layout to the actual appliances and finishes. “The kitchen layout changed several times throughout the process, and it certainly helped that our builder, Don Jones [of Craig Construction], was once a chef!” she explains. “We really prioritized flow and functionality first, then let the design follow.”

Blue cabinetry ties in with the stove while bronze hardware does the same with the custom patinated brass hood, which warms everything up and will only get better-looking with age, as will the quartz countertops. The vintage plates on the wall add personality and style to this workhorse space.

In the wine cellar and tasting room, the architectural elements were quite linear, so Matthews opted for an arched doorway to create some movement. “We loved the idea of the temperature controlled wine cellar having a cavernous feel, which is why we chose to bring natural stone into the interior,” she explains.

Another favorite room of Matthews’, she especially loves the bookcase since it gives the cozy room an almost historic, collected feel. To add height and balance the scale of the bookshelves, she hung a tapestry rug above the bed, creating a layered, timeless escape for the homeowners.

The wallpaper, paired with the ruched velvet bed frame, adds romantic appeal to this guest bedroom. Vintage artworks and furniture, like the trunk, lend a collected feel, bringing the space to life. “The vintage sketches were carefully framed and hung from brass chains, adding a nod to the past and giving the room a sense of history,” the designer explains.

With over a decade in the design industry, McKenzie Matthews firmly believes good design should feel effortless and evolve over time. Matthews is the founder and principal designer of Coven Haus, a boutique interior design studio based in Utah and serving clients nationwide. The studio’s mission is to bring its clients’ visions of home to life through thoughtful design, collaboration, and authentic representations.

#6780. James Talarico’s Political-Powerhouse Girlfriend, Brianna Menard, Is Also a Master Thrifter

The 2026 midterm elections brought a blue wave of record-breaking wins. Among the most monumental was James Talarico, who became the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Texas since 1988.

But his historic win is not all the internet has been talking about. At his celebratory Election Night event in Austin, Texas, the 37-year-old senator-elect was joined by his girlfriend, Brianna Menard, who was previously his chief of staff. Days later, the two attended a University of Texas football game—to which Menard wore a corduroy minidress she thrifted the week before—and the moment went viral across social media. (Even better, Talarico’s mom was the one who shared the photo of the couple at the game that quickly got traction on X.)

Chalk it up to her political prowess, clear sense of style, or the fact that she looks like an Instagram baddie, but some fans have even gone as far as to declare the pair this generation’s John F. Kennedy and Jacqueline Kennedy.

The couple first met in 2022, when Menard joined the politician’s team as chief of staff, and their relationship eventually turned romantic. Menard has been by Talarico’s side throughout his Senate campaign, accompanying him to the polls on Election Day in November and later joining him onstage to celebrate his historic victory.

So, who is Brianna Menard? Ahead, everything to know about Talarico’s accomplished and stylish girlfriend.

Menard is a born-and-raised Texan. She attended and graduated from the University of Texas at Austin, where she studied government.

In 2022, Menard was hired as Talarico’s chief of staff. According to reports, the two didn’t begin dating until a year later, after which Menard left her role working for the politician. In August 2026, Talarico’s campaign confirmed the couple’s relationship. “Four years ago, after he and his then-chief of staff developed feelings for each other and started dating, she left the office to pursue other opportunities,” a Talarico campaign spokesman told the New York Times.

After leaving Talarico’s office, Menard worked on the campaign for Rep. Salman Bhojani, the first Muslim member of the Texas legislature, and eventually became his chief of staff.

Menard is currently the director of TEXPAC and political education at the Texas Medical Association. According to her bio on the organization’s site, before stepping into the role, she had a decade of experience working in the Texas Legislature and previously served as executive director of the Early Childhood Caucus of the Texas House, where she led bipartisan efforts to “advance early learning, childcare access, workforce development, and healthcare affordability.”

Menard’s bio also lists her as the Board Secretary for Wheatsville Food Co-op and a member of the City of Austin’s Early Childhood Council.

According to a now-deleted bio on the Wheatsville Food Co-Op site, where she currently serves as Board Secretary, Menard called herself a “foodie and a committed vegan” who loves cooking. In the welcome post, she also revealed her love of yoga, dancing, and cuddling her cat named Zia.

“I’ve spent my career serving in the Texas Legislature and working on political campaigns across the state with the goal of making Texas a healthier and more equitable home for all of us,” she wrote in the post.

Menard joined Talarico at the polls to vote early in the midterm elections. On November 3, she also joined Talarico’s Election Night event in Austin, where she congratulated the Senator-elect on stage following his historic win. The couple shared a sweet hug and kiss to celebrate.
